questions.knowledge_point: Writing a Vector in a Different Basis Given a Linear Relationship Between Two Bases
questions.problem: Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ be a basis of ${R}^{2}$ and $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}].$ What are the coordinates of $x$ relative to the basis $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}},$ where ${c}_{1}=-{b}_{2}$ and ${c}_{2}={b}_{2}-{b}_{1}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We are given that

$$
{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}=-{b}_{2} \\ {c}_{2}={b}_{2}-{b}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we express the $b$'s in terms of $c$'s. From the first equation, we get 

$$
{b}_{2}=-{c}_{1}.
$$

Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain

$$
{c}_{2}=-{c}_{1}-{b}_{1}\,⟹\,{b}_{1}=-{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}.
$$

Since $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]$, we can write the vector $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =3{b}_{1}+5{b}_{2} \\  & =3(-{c}_{1}-{c}_{2})+5(-{c}_{1}) \\  & =-3{c}_{1}-3{c}_{2}-5{c}_{1} \\  & =-8{c}_{1}-3{c}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ -3\end{aligned}]$

questions.knowledge_point: Writing a Vector in a Different Basis Given a Linear Relationship Between Two Bases
questions.problem: Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ be a basis of ${R}^{2}$ and $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$ What are the coordinates of $x$ relative to the basis $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}},$ where ${c}_{1}={b}_{1}-\frac{1}{2}{b}_{2}$ and ${c}_{2}={b}_{2}-\frac{1}{2}{b}_{1}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We are given that

$$
{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}={b}_{1}-\frac{1}{2}{b}_{2} \\ {c}_{2}={b}_{2}-\frac{1}{2}{b}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we express the $b$'s in terms of $c$'s. Multiplying the second equation by $2$ and adding the equations, we get 

$$
{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2}=\frac{3}{2}{b}_{2}\,⟹\,{b}_{2}=\frac{2}{3}{c}_{1}+\frac{4}{3}{c}_{2}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}-\frac{1}{2}(\frac{2}{3}{c}_{1}+\frac{4}{3}{c}_{2})\,⟹\,{b}_{1}=\frac{4}{3}{c}_{1}+\frac{2}{3}{c}_{2}.
$$

Since $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]$, we can write the vector $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={b}_{1}+4{b}_{2} \\  & =(\frac{4}{3}{c}_{1}+\frac{2}{3}{c}_{2})+4(\frac{2}{3}{c}_{1}+\frac{4}{3}{c}_{2}) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}{c}_{1}+\frac{2}{3}{c}_{2}+\frac{8}{3}{c}_{1}+\frac{16}{3}{c}_{2} \\  & =4{c}_{1}+6{c}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6\end{aligned}].$

questions.knowledge_point: Writing a Two-Dimensional Vector in a Different Basis
questions.problem: Let $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$ be a basis of ${R}^{2}$ and $[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ What are the coordinates of $x$ relative to the basis $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}},$ where ${b}_{1}={c}_{2}$ and ${b}_{2}=-{c}_{1}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$, we can write $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2} \\  & =2{c}_{2}-{c}_{1} \\  & =2{c}_{2}+(-{c}_{1}) \\  & =2{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

provenance.kp_title: Writing a Two-Dimensional Vector in a Different Basis
